PUBLIC RESPONSE: 28 and 74

The poem is a double sestina, so the final three-line envoi should echo the six repeated end-words. In the given version, lines 73 and 75 already supply mountains/valleys and morning/evening, but line 74 only gives music and leaves “forests” missing from the envoi. Line 28 is the forest-bearing line that also has the same “Long since” opening as line 74, so it is the most likely stray line from the envoi. Swapping 28 and 74 restores the missing forest echo in the final triad and returns the “Long since, alas…” line to the anaphoric “Long since” sequence in Strephon’s stanza. Thus the two lines that appear to have been swapped are 28 and 74.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The swapped lines are 24 and 74. The envoi (73–75) should close on the terminal words valleys, music, evening; line 74 as given repeats the body’s “Long since…” lament and leaves the envoi without the needed “vales/music” closure. Line 24, “And fill the vales with cries instead of music,” is the true envoi line. Moving line 74 back to the fourth stanza also restores the terminal “music” after the “Heartbroken…” line and keeps the sestina’s end-word sequence intact. The apparent awkwardness at 25 is not a swap; “These forests” is being used collectively with “Hath” in early modern idiom.

12.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: 15 and 21. The sestina’s repeated end-word pattern is still intact here—both lines end in “music”—so the break is not in the terminal words themselves but in the alternating speaker-parallel. Strephon’s stanza has paired “I, that was once…” lines at 13 and 15; Klaius’s corresponding stanza has the same construction at 19 and 21. The second of these in each speaker’s sequence should match that speaker’s former condition: Strephon’s should be his past esteem for music, while Klaius’s should be his former role as “the music of these valleys.” In the modified text these are interchanged: line 21’s valley-music line belongs with Strephon’s forest/sport/banishment sequence, and line 15’s “esteemed for pleasant music” belongs with Klaius’s hunting/morning/darkening sequence. Swapping 15 and 21 restores the intended parallel without disturbing the end-word cycle.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: 25 and 28. The disruption is in Strephon’s fifth stanza. Lines 26–27 (“Hath made itself a crier of the morning, / And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains”) clearly depend on a singular subject introduced at line 25. In the modified text, line 25 is the stray fragment “These forests eke, made wretched by our music,” which does not fit that syntax. The line that belongs there is the opening of the “Long since” sequence currently at line 28, “Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests;” swapping 25 and 28 restores the stanza’s internal anaphora and grammatical progression.
